solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cardinal, no Saint, needing drink

indicators.note: saying 'no' to something turns it away, so a letter is refused entry

blocks.note: someone needing a drink is thirsty
S is the standard abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A cardinal of the Church, stripped of sainthood, reaching for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' looks like a churchman; here it is a cardinal number, THIRTY, which is THIRSTY once its S goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal numbers are the counting numbers, so any of them, thirty included, is a cardinal.

clue.text: Short-term tenant in trouble with IRS

indicators.note: things in trouble are thrown into disorder, so the letters get jumbled

blocks.note: taken letter for letter
taken letter for letter; the US tax service

explanation.surface: A tenant on a short lease finds themselves in hot water with the American tax authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short-term tenant' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops after 'Short-term', and the tenant joins IRS as the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something transient lasts only a brief while, which is what a short-term arrangement does.

clue.text: What acts as a connection is time — hours add up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reads the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the usual abbreviation for time
h is the abbreviation for hours
to add is to sum

explanation.surface: Someone musing that time is the link between things as the hours pile up.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'hours add up' look like a comment on time; it is H plus SUM written upward.
explanation.definitionFit: An isthmus is a narrow neck of land joining two larger landmasses, so it serves as a link.

clue.text: Cast can read out loud

indicators.note: reading something out loud means we go by how it sounds, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: the can and the throne are both slang for the lavatory

explanation.surface: A theatre cast being asked whether they can read their lines out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast can read' looks like a question about actors; 'Cast' is the past participle of throw, and 'can' is lavatory slang, the throne.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast a stone is to throw it, so something cast has been thrown.

clue.text: Plant’s beginning to hold strike with fear for marine plant

indicators.note: whatever holds something keeps it inside, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: every plant begins as a seed
to awe someone is to fill them with dread

explanation.surface: Botanical musing about how a plant starts life and what frightens it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant’s beginning' tempts a solver to take the first letter P; here it means the seed from which a plant begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Seaweed is the ordinary name for algae growing in the ocean, the commonest example of vegetation living there.

clue.text: Inside measurement is key for collar

indicators.note: a thing inside something else is surrounded by it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a size is a measurement, as of clothing
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: A tailor explaining that the inside neck measurement is what matters when fitting a shirt collar.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all shirt-making, but 'collar' is a verb: police collar a suspect. E is one of the musical keys.
explanation.definitionFit: To collar someone is informal for grabbing or arresting them, the same as taking hold.

clue.text: Exhausted learner coming in to land very well

indicators.note: an exhausted thing is emptied out, so only its outside letters stay
arriving into a place puts you inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: to land, as a bird does on a branch, is to alight
the first and last letters of learner

explanation.surface: A worn-out learner pilot coming in to land and doing it very well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhausted learner' looks like the usual L; it is the whole word with its middle emptied, LR, which goes into ALIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are spoken agreement, used to accept a suggestion, so one serves in place of the other.

clue.text: Female workers implicated in Watergate scandal

indicators.note: someone implicated in an affair is caught up inside it, so the letters sit within the words

blocks.note: found straddling the two words, from the fourth letter of the first

explanation.surface: Some women staff members caught up in the Nixon-era political scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests secretaries in the Watergate affair; the answer is a zoological term for worker ants, lurking across the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergates are worker ants, which are sterile females, so these are insect workers of the female sex.

clue.text: Extremist papers served up the same thing

indicators.note: in a down clue, being served up sends the letters upward, reading bottom to top

blocks.note: OTT, over the top, describes anything extreme
identity papers are ID

explanation.surface: Radical newspapers keep dishing out the same old stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' suggests newspapers, but it is ID, identity papers; OTT (over the top) is British shorthand for excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Ditto is used to repeat what was just said or written, meaning identical to the previous item.

clue.text: Court in support over proposed US constitutional amendment and the like

indicators.note: placing one thing in another puts it inside
in a down clue, turned over means flipped end to end

blocks.note: a golf tee supports the ball
CT is the abbreviation for court
the Equal Rights Amendment, proposed but never ratified

explanation.surface: A court case in support of a proposed amendment to the US constitution.
explanation.walkthrough: CT goes into TEE as TE-CT-E, which is turned over to ETCET; the ERA is the Equal Rights Amendment. The 'and' is shared: the definition is 'and the like'.
explanation.definitionFit: Et cetera is Latin for 'and other things', used to end a list with similar items.

clue.text: Knock back roll filled with cold ham?

indicators.note: whatever is filled has something put inside it
knocking something back sends it the other way

blocks.note: a rota is a roll or roster of duties
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Refusing a bread roll stuffed with cold ham.
explanation.walkthrough: The sandwich misleads: 'roll' is ROTA, the British word for a duty roster, and 'ham' is an overacting performer. The question mark flags that a ham is only one kind of actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A ham is a performer who overacts, so a ham is one example of a thespian.

clue.text: In the trunk area, red blazer is snug, restricting one in everything

definitions.text: In the trunk area, red blazer

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one piece closes round another
a thing placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: a snug fit is a tight one
everything is all
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone snug in a red blazer, though the talk of a trunk sounds like an elephant or luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes into ALL, and that goes into TIGHT. The 'trunk' is the American word for a car's boot, and the 'red blazer' is a glowing lamp, not a jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: Rear car lamps glow red at the back of the vehicle, beside the boot, so the lamp there is that glowing red thing.

clue.text: Home sewer burst in an unidentified location

indicators.note: something that bursts flies apart, so the letters scatter into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A household drain has ruptured, and nobody can tell where.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' reads as a drain, though it could equally be someone who sews; either way it is only letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb places something at a spot not specified, exactly what the phrase describes.

clue.text: Scored opening runs into covers

indicators.note: a cover goes over and round something, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: taken as written
R for runs, as on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: Cricket: an opening batsman scored runs into the covers, a fielding area on the off side.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is cricket, where covers is a fielding position and an opener scores runs; 'Scored opening' is instead a piece of music at the start of a song.
explanation.definitionFit: A song's intro is the introductory passage of music, written out in the score before the main part.

clue.text: Like to ogle cut sandwiches and a piece of cake

indicators.note: cutting trims something short, so its final letter drops away
sandwiching puts a filling between two outer slices

blocks.note: to ogle is to eye, here cut short
like and as both compare

explanation.surface: Someone who likes to eye up the cut sandwiches and a slice of cake at tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Tea-time food fills the surface, and 'sandwiches' turns out to be a verb. EYE loses its last letter and takes AS inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a task a piece of cake is an idiom for saying it is simple to do.

clue.text: Traditional gear was in the van — the person driving starts off jerkily

indicators.note: the driver sits up front, so this piece leads what follows
with their starts off, words lose their opening letters
a jerky ride throws things about, so the letters are shaken up

blocks.note: to be in the van (vanguard) is to lead
each word loses its first letter: tHE pERSON

explanation.surface: Someone in the van as the driver pulls away with a lurch.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'van' is the vanguard, not a vehicle; being in front is leading. The rest shuffled gives ERHOSEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Lederhosen are the leather shorts of Bavarian and Alpine folk costume, national dress worn at festivals.

clue.text: One quickly passes on first show of Edinburgh fringe after parking takes an age

indicators.note: the first show of anything is its opening, so only the initial letter counts
one thing coming after another fixes their order

blocks.note: initial letter of Edinburgh
P is the road-sign symbol for parking
a hem is a border or fringe of cloth
an era is an age

explanation.surface: A visitor to the Edinburgh Fringe festival who spends ages trying to park.
explanation.walkthrough: The Edinburgh Fringe is an arts festival, but 'fringe' is just HEM. Ephemera is the mayfly genus, whose adults live about a day.
explanation.definitionFit: A mayfly dies within hours of reaching adulthood, so it is a creature whose life is over fast.

clue.text: One proposing to get married in a prominent landmark south of New Orleans initially

indicators.note: in a down clue, south of means placed beneath, so that piece comes later
initially means at the start, so only the first letters are wanted

blocks.note: the initials of New Orleans
m. is the abbreviation for married
taken as written
a tor is a rocky hill standing out on a moor

explanation.surface: A proposal of marriage at a famous landmark somewhere south of New Orleans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proposing' and 'married' suggest a wedding, but the proposing is of a candidate. A tor is a craggy hilltop, common on Dartmoor in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominator puts forward a candidate's name for office or an award, which is proposing them.

clue.text: Distress caused by brief violent behaviour one evening

indicators.note: a brief version is cut short, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: aggro, trimmed of its last letter
Roman numeral one
eve is an old word for evening

explanation.surface: Upset caused by a short burst of violence one night.
explanation.walkthrough: Aggro is British slang for aggressive or violent behaviour, especially fighting.
explanation.definitionFit: To aggrieve someone is to wrong them and leave them upset, the verb sense of causing distress.

clue.text: My photo turned out grainier with a mobile imaging technique

indicators.note: whatever is turned out is thrown out, so letters are ejected
mobile means free to move, so the letters rearrange

blocks.note: taken as written
the word with its tail INIER thrown out

explanation.surface: Complaining that a picture taken on a phone came out grainy.
explanation.walkthrough: The mobile phone and the grainy picture are one scene; 'mobile' is the anagram signal. The parse of 'grainier' is loose: only its first three letters join the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomography builds pictures of the body's interior slice by slice, as in CT scans, a medical scanning method.

clue.text: It could drive many people mad missing out on promotion, challenging in vain

indicators.note: missing out on something means going without it, so those letters are lost
a challenging arrangement is a troubled, disputed one, so the letters are unsettled

blocks.note: mad without its second part
an ad is a promotion
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Being passed over for promotion drives many people mad as they appeal in vain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive many people mad' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'people': the vehicle drives, meaning carries, a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A minivan is a passenger vehicle built to carry a large family or group, so it transports several travellers.

clue.text: Mathematical expressions only half written down in class

indicators.note: writing down only half means the rest is never put on paper

blocks.note: formulae are mathematical expressions; its first half is kept

explanation.surface: A pupil in maths class only managing to copy down half the formulae.
explanation.walkthrough: A form is a British school class or year group, as in 'the sixth form'.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools a form is a group of pupils taught together, the same as a school year group.

clue.text: This could cause rustiness in old worker, say, after eleven days

indicators.note: coming after something places it later in the sequence

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
XI is Roman eleven, and also a cricket or football team
d is the abbreviation for days
the ant is the crossword's standard worker, 'say' marking an example

explanation.surface: An old employee who gets rusty after eleven days away from the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rustiness in old worker' reads as someone out of practice; the definition is chemical, with 'in' only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen, and an oxidant is the agent that drives such a reaction.

clue.text: Force European to stand in for a year in an English resort

indicators.note: a stand-in takes another's place, so one piece swaps with another

blocks.note: Torquay, a seaside town in Devon
A plus Y for year
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European being made to fill in for a year at an English seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Torquay is a seaside resort in Devon, south-west England. 'Force' looks like a verb opening the sentence; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Torque is a twisting or turning physical effect that makes something rotate, a rotational counterpart of push or pull.

clue.text: Entrance to house new for one delivering gift?

indicators.note: housing something means giving it a place inside

blocks.note: a door is an entrance
N for new

explanation.surface: The front door of a new house, where someone is dropping off a present.
explanation.walkthrough: The courier at the door is a decoy; a donor gives rather than delivers, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A donor is someone who hands over a gift, whether money, blood or an organ, to others.

clue.text: Contrary lad concluding early medical discharge

indicators.note: finishing early means the last letter never arrives
contrary means running the opposite way, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: a lad is a boy, stopped a letter short
medical cut to its first three letters

explanation.surface: A stubborn young soldier leaving the army early on medical grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medical discharge' looks like the definition, but only 'discharge' is. Demob is British informal for demobilisation, release from the forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Being demobbed means being released from military service, which is a discharge from the army.

clue.text: Mass evacuation following company disturbance

indicators.note: what follows comes behind, so that piece goes second

blocks.note: Co. is short for company
m is the symbol for mass
a motion is a bowel movement

explanation.surface: A whole firm being evacuated from its building in a mass exodus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass evacuation' reads as a crowd leaving a building; it is M plus a lavatorial motion.
explanation.definitionFit: A commotion is a noisy, confused uproar, one of many words for a disturbance.

clue.text: Put out daughter’s head of cabbage in rubbish

indicators.note: a head is at the top, so only the first letter is taken
read as 'is': one letter is the other, so one takes over the other's place

blocks.note: dross is worthless waste
D for daughter
first letter of cabbage

explanation.surface: A daughter putting out the rubbish, cabbage leaves and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as taking the bins out; it means annoyed. D in DROSS becomes C.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone put out is irritated or offended, which is what being cross means.

clue.text: Film buff’s second contender to collect for example Oscar

indicators.note: collecting things gathers them in, so pieces go inside

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second
one who vies is a vier
e.g. means for example
O in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A cinema enthusiast talking about the runner-up in the race for an Oscar.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar is the Academy Award in the surface and a letter of the NATO phonetic alphabet in the wordplay; 'contender' means one who vies.
explanation.definitionFit: A cinema enthusiast is someone who regularly goes to see pictures, so a regular at the pictures.

clue.text: Computer modeller and designer

blocks.note: a quantitative analyst who builds numerical models in finance
the London fashion designer Mary of the 1960s, famed for the miniskirt

explanation.walkthrough: Mary Quant was the British fashion designer credited with popularising the miniskirt; a quant is finance jargon for a numbers analyst.
explanation.definitionFit: Quantitative analysts build mathematical simulations on software, and Mary Quant created clothes.

clue.text: South African nurses nitpick on emptying small potty

indicators.note: emptying something clears out its middle, leaving just its outer shell
to nurse is to cradle something in your arms, holding it inside

blocks.note: a Boer is an Afrikaner, a South African of Dutch descent
first and last letters of nitpick
S for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: South African nurses fussing over an emptied chamber pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potty' looks like a child's pot, and 'nurses' like hospital staff; potty is British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal British slang for mad or crazy, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Riot in court compound is initiated by judge

indicators.note: being initiated by something means it comes at the start

blocks.note: J for judge
an ester is a chemical compound

explanation.surface: A disturbance breaks out in a courtroom compound, started by the judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riot in court' looks like a courtroom disturbance; a riot is also a hilarious person, and the court is a royal one.
explanation.definitionFit: A court jester was the king's fool, so he was the funny person at the royal household.
